cases.case_name: State ex rel Dept. of Human Services v. Simmons
cases.holding: Reversing termination, the court held the State had not proved by clear and convincing evidence that mother's mental illness and past substance addiction made her unfit at the time of the termination trial, the only time frame that matters.
cases.quote: On this record, there is not clear and convincing evidence of a present drug abuse problem that would render mother unfit at the time of the termination trial.

relevance.OUT-02: Sets the Oregon Supreme Court's controlling application of the clear-and-convincing unfitness standard, measured at the time of the termination trial rather than on historical conduct.
relevance.FAIL-01: Demonstrates appellate reversal of a termination judgment where the agency's evidence of unfitness was stale and legally insufficient.

cases.case_name: State ex rel SOSCF v. Stillman
cases.holding: The court affirmed reversal of termination, construing ORS 419B.504 to require a two-part showing — present unfitness from seriously detrimental conduct or condition, and improbability of integration within a reasonable time — and holding an incarcerated father's drug history did not make him presently unfit.
cases.quote: ORS 419B.504 sets out a two-part test for determining whether to terminate parental rights, both parts of which must be met before the court orders termination.

relevance.OUT-02: This is the leading Oregon Supreme Court construction of the ORS 419B.504 unfitness ground, and the source of the two-part test every later Oregon termination case applies.

cases.case_name: State ex rel Dept. of Human Services v. Smith
cases.holding: Reversing two terminations, the court held that DHS may not condition return of a child on compliance with service demands untethered to statutory unfitness, and that every fact supporting termination must be proved to a high probability.
cases.quote: Under that standard, the court must find that the evidence establishes that the truth of the facts asserted is highly probable.

relevance.ACT-01: Limits how far the agency may push a parent into voluntary services: non-compliance with agency-imposed conditions that are not tied to a statutory ground cannot itself justify keeping or removing a child.
relevance.ACT-02: Defines the outer bound of court-ordered service plans — the conditions exacted of a parent must bear on statutory unfitness, not on the agency's preferred standard of parenting.
relevance.DEC-06: Supports resolving cases without escalation where the agency's concerns do not rise to a statutory ground for state intervention.
relevance.OUT-01: Reinforces that reunification must follow once the statutory basis is unproven, regardless of a parent's failure to satisfy agency service demands.

cases.case_name: Dept. of Human Services v. T. M. D.
cases.holding: The court held there is no statutory presumption or preference favoring termination over permanent guardianship, that the department bears the full burden on best interests, and on this record termination was not in the child's best interest.
cases.quote: The department must prove only that that the parent's conduct justifies termination and that the best interest of the child will be served by termination.

relevance.OUT-02: Controls the best-interests half of an Oregon termination case and rejects any thumb on the scale in favor of adoption over less drastic permanency.
relevance.OUT-03: Establishes that permanent guardianship is a legitimate competing permanency option that the court must weigh against termination on the evidence presented.

cases.case_name: Dept. of Human Services v. S. J. M.
cases.holding: Once DHS proves the ORS 419B.476 requirements for changing a permanency plan away from reunification, the burden shifts to the party invoking the ORS 419B.498(2) escape clause to prove a 'compelling reason' not to file a termination petition.
cases.quote: it was parents' burden, as the parties seeking to invoke the escape clause, to show that there was a "compelling reason" under ORS 419B.498(2)

relevance.DEC-06: Fixes who must prove what at the fork between continuing reunification services and moving to a termination track.
relevance.ACT-04: Addresses relative foster placement with a maternal aunt and the statutory 'compelling reason' grounds that include preserving sibling attachments.
relevance.OUT-01: Defines the burden allocation that determines whether reunification remains the plan after a permanency hearing.
relevance.OUT-03: Frames when an alternative permanent plan, rather than adoption, is 'better suited' to the child's health and safety needs.
relevance.PMC-03: The escape-clause statute the court construes expressly turns in part on a prior determination by the court or local citizen review board that reasonable or active efforts were not made.

cases.case_name: Dept. of Human Services v. T. L.
cases.holding: The court held that a parent may raise an unpreserved inadequate-assistance-of-counsel claim on direct appeal from a permanency judgment changing the plan from reunification to guardianship or APPLA, and remanded for an evidentiary record.
cases.quote: counsel appointed pursuant to ORS 419B.205 must be adequate, with adequacy determined using a standard of fundamental fairness

relevance.FAIL-01: Supplies the Oregon route for undoing a permanency judgment entered after counsel failed the parent, without waiting for a collateral ORS 419B.923 motion.
relevance.OUT-01: Protects the reunification plan by making counsel's adequacy reviewable at the moment the plan is changed away from return to parent.
relevance.OUT-03: Applies specifically to judgments moving the permanent plan to guardianship or another planned permanent living arrangement.

cases.case_name: Dept. of Human Services v. C. M. H.
cases.holding: The court held the juvenile court's 'exclusive original jurisdiction' under ORS 419B.100(1) is subject matter jurisdiction that attaches from the allegations and relief sought in a pending petition, and is not conditioned on a wardship determination.
cases.quote: The juvenile court had subject matter jurisdiction in this case.

relevance.DEC-05: Settles what the filing of a dependency petition does and does not confer on the juvenile court, which is the threshold question whenever the agency opens a case.
relevance.INP-04: Governs the juvenile court's authority to act on collateral matters, including parentage, once a dependency petition invokes its jurisdiction.
relevance.INP-05: Clarifies that jurisdiction turns on the petition's allegations rather than on who set the case in motion or on a later wardship finding.

cases.case_name: State ex rel Dept. of Human Services v. W. P.
cases.holding: Weighing deterrence against child safety, the court held that evidence obtained through an unlawful search is not subject to exclusion in a juvenile dependency proceeding.
cases.quote: we conclude that the federal exclusionary rule does not apply in juvenile dependency proceedings

relevance.DEC-02: Tells a parent that the fruits of an unlawful search may still be used to open and prove a dependency case, even though the search itself may support other remedies.
relevance.DEC-05: Directly governs a motion to suppress filed in response to a dependency petition.
relevance.FAIL-01: Marks the limits of the suppression remedy as a way to attack an agency's evidentiary foundation in juvenile court.
relevance.INP-10: Bears on escalation from investigation to petition where the investigative evidence was unlawfully gathered.

cases.case_name: State ex rel Juv. Dept. v. Geist
cases.holding: The court held that a parent may raise inadequate assistance of appointed counsel on direct appeal from a termination judgment, judged by a due process standard of fundamental fairness, though on this record counsel was adequate.
cases.quote: We hold that such claims may be reviewed on direct appeal.

relevance.FAIL-01: This is the foundational Oregon authority permitting a parent to overturn a juvenile judgment because appointed counsel was inadequate, and the source of the 'fundamental fairness' standard later extended in T. L.

cases.case_name: Dept. of Human Services v. A. B.
cases.holding: The court held that when wardship is terminated during an appeal, the department — not the parent — bears the burden of proving the jurisdictional judgment will have no practical effect, and here it carried that burden.
cases.quote: The burden is on the department to prove that a jurisdictional judgment will have no practical effect on the rights of the parties and is therefore moot.

relevance.DEC-03: Recognizes and then measures the stigma and collateral consequences a parent claims from a founded jurisdictional finding.
relevance.DEC-05: Controls whether a parent can still challenge the petition-based jurisdictional judgment after the agency closes the case.
relevance.OUT-05: Governs the mootness consequences of dismissal or termination of wardship for a pending appeal.
relevance.PMC-06: Provides the Oregon Supreme Court's framework for assessing whether recorded agency findings continue to burden a family after case closure — the empirical question behind transparency analysis.

cases.case_name: Dept. of Human Services v. S. M.
cases.holding: The court affirmed that DHS, as the children's court-appointed legal guardian, had statutory authority to consent to immunizations over the parents' objection, subject to its own rules requiring notice and an opportunity for the parents to be heard in juvenile court.
cases.quote: Indeed, immunization is less invasive and more routine than surgery, which DHS specifically may authorize as the wards' legal guardian.

relevance.ACT-02: Shows how court-ordered guardianship converts into concrete agency decision-making authority over a ward and what procedural checks constrain it.
relevance.ACT-03: Explains the legal consequences of the custody-and-guardianship order that accompanies foster placement.
relevance.ACT-05: Identifies the juvenile-court process by which a parent may contest a protective agency decision short of changing the placement.
relevance.ACT-06: Directly resolves the scope of DHS's authority to authorize medical care for a ward over parental objection.
relevance.INP-05: Frames the residual rights a parent retains to invoke the juvenile court after voluntarily admitting jurisdictional allegations.

cases.case_name: Dept. of Human Services v. C. H.
cases.holding: The court held that reasonable efforts under ORS 419B.476 are assessed on the totality of the circumstances, including whether services were tailored to the family's needs, and affirmed the change of plan to adoption.
cases.quote: we conclude that the juvenile court did not err as a matter of law in determining that DHS's efforts were reasonable under ORS 419B.476

relevance.OUT-01: This is the current Oregon Supreme Court standard for judging whether the agency did enough to make safe return home possible.
relevance.ACT-01: Requires the service offer itself to be evaluated for fit with the family's actual needs.
relevance.ACT-02: Supplies the legal test against which an ordered service plan is measured at each permanency hearing.
relevance.ACT-03: Sets the reasonable-efforts finding that federal Title IV-E funding and continued foster placement depend on.
relevance.DEC-06: Determines whether the case stays on a reunification track or moves toward termination.
relevance.PMC-01: The totality-of-circumstances reasonable-efforts inquiry is the state-court analogue of the CFSR safety and permanency measures.
relevance.PMC-03: Judicial reasonable-efforts findings are the record that citizen review bodies examine when auditing agency performance.
relevance.FAIL-05: The parents argued reasonable efforts must account for the needs of parents with disabilities, and the court evaluated DHS's insensitivity to a race-related conflict over the child's hair as part of the totality.

cases.case_name: Dept. of Human Services v. Y. B.
cases.holding: The court held that a juvenile court's 'sufficient progress' determination under ORS 419B.476(2)(a) is a legal conclusion reviewed for legal error, not a finding of fact, and affirmed the change of plan to guardianship.
cases.quote: Thus, the text of the statute suggests that the juvenile court's determinations of "reasonable efforts" and "sufficient progress" are legal conclusions.

relevance.OUT-01: Fixes the standard of appellate review for the finding that most often ends a reunification plan in Oregon.
relevance.DEC-06: Governs the legal characterization of the permanency determination that decides whether the case leaves the reunification track.
relevance.ACT-02: Measures a parent's progress on the ordered service plan as a question of law rather than an unreviewable fact finding.

cases.case_name: Dept. of Human Services v. T. J. N.
cases.holding: The court held the Court of Appeals erred in dismissing the parents' placement appeals as moot because the moving party had not persuaded the court that dismissal was warranted, though the appeals had since become moot for other reasons.
cases.quote: But unless the moving party "persuades the appellate court that the dismissal is warranted," the appeal is not moot.

relevance.OUT-05: Governs when a dependency appeal survives intervening dismissal or supersession of the underlying judgment, and places the persuasion burden on the party seeking dismissal.

cases.case_name: State ex rel Dugan v. Tiktin
cases.holding: The court held a trial court may not delegate to the prosecuting district attorney the in camera review of confidential child-welfare agency files, but must conduct that review itself.
cases.quote: We hold that the trial court may not delegate in camera review, but must itself perform that duty.

relevance.FAIL-06: Shows that confidentiality of child-welfare records is enforced by judicial gatekeeping, not by agency or prosecutor discretion.
relevance.PMC-05: Establishes the Oregon procedure for court-supervised disclosure of otherwise confidential child-protection files.

cases.case_name: Kasliner v. Dept. of Human Services
cases.holding: The court affirmed a judgment remanding a DHS 'founded' child-abuse determination, holding the circuit court properly found the investigation biased and the founded determination unsupported by substantial evidence, and properly awarded attorney fees.
cases.quote: In this case, the circuit court expressly found that DHS had conducted a biased investigation, a finding that the circuit court in Querbach did not make.

relevance.DEC-01: Shows that an investigation which does not pursue exculpatory or alternative explanations cannot support a disposition either way.
relevance.DEC-03: This is the leading recent Oregon decision on judicial review of a DHS 'founded' abuse determination issued as an order in other than a contested case.
relevance.INP-01: Traces the path from a report of abuse through the agency investigation that decides whether the reported person is labeled an abuser.
relevance.INP-02: Applies to non-mandated reports as well, since the founded/unfounded process does not turn on the reporter's status.
relevance.INP-06: Governs the quality of investigation owed after a hotline report before the agency may make a founded finding.
relevance.INP-10: Sets out what the agency must do once a screened report is escalated to a full investigation, including obtaining collateral evidence.
relevance.FAIL-01: A working example of a court vacating an agency child-abuse finding for bias and lack of substantial evidence.

cases.case_name: Pamplin Media Group v. City of Salem
cases.holding: The court held that ORS 419B.035's exclusion of child-abuse reports and records from disclosure does not sweep in an arrest record merely because the underlying investigation began as a child-abuse report, and the city failed to carry its burden of proving exemption.
cases.quote: On both parties' motions for summary judgment, the city bore the burden of proving that the requested records were exempt from disclosure.

relevance.FAIL-06: Directly rejects an agency's attempt to use the child-abuse confidentiality statute as a blanket shield against public records disclosure.
relevance.PMC-05: This is the controlling Oregon authority on the scope of the ORS 419B.035 exclusion in a public records request, and places the burden of proving exemption on the government.
relevance.INP-01: Construes ORS 419B.010 to 419B.050 — the mandatory reporting and investigation provisions — to define what is and is not a confidential 'report of child abuse.'
relevance.INP-02: Applies equally to records generated by non-mandated reports routed into the same investigative stream.
relevance.INP-03: Addresses records held by a police agency that received and acted on a child-abuse report.
relevance.INP-06: Defines the confidentiality that attaches, and does not attach, to records generated from hotline and other abuse reports.
relevance.DEC-03: Limits how far an agency may extend confidentiality over the record trail supporting an abuse determination.

cases.case_name: State v. L. P. L. O.
cases.holding: The court held a youth's own dependency petition was not mooted by his turning 18, that the UCCJEA supplied subject matter jurisdiction, and that the juvenile court was required on its findings to take dependency jurisdiction over him.
cases.quote: We conclude that petitioner's appeal is not moot, there is subject matter jurisdiction under the UCCJEA, and petitioner is within the court's dependency jurisdiction.

relevance.OUT-04: Holds that reaching age 18 does not extinguish the appeal or the juvenile court's ability to act, the core question for youth seeking care past majority.
relevance.INP-04: Addresses the juvenile court's obligation to act on a petition presented to it rather than declining jurisdiction as a matter of discretion.
relevance.INP-05: This is the Oregon case on a young person petitioning on his own behalf for dependency jurisdiction and services.

cases.case_name: State ex rel Juv. Dept. v. Smith
cases.holding: The court affirmed appointment of an independent health-care guardian for a severely disabled ward with authority to withhold or withdraw life-sustaining procedures over the mother's objection, emphasizing the stringency of the statutory criteria where a guardian displaces a parent.
cases.quote: Further, we emphasize that, despite the imprecision of the statutory language, the criterion that the statute establishes is stringent, at least where the guardian replaces a minor's parent.

relevance.ACT-06: This is the Oregon authority on court authorization of grave medical decisions for a child in agency custody over a parent's objection, and on how demanding the showing must be.
relevance.INP-07: Arises directly from the medical setting and defines who may consent to or refuse treatment for a ward once the health-care system raises the issue.

cases.case_name: Dept. of Human Services v. M. P.
cases.holding: The court held a protective custody order under ORS 419B.150 is not an 'initial child custody determination' and the supporting declaration is not the first pleading, so the dependency proceeding commenced when the petition was filed, defeating UCCJEA home-state jurisdiction.
cases.quote: An issued but unexecuted protective custody order does not trigger the juvenile court's jurisdiction or commence any time period during which a petition must be filed.

relevance.INP-12: This is the most detailed recent Oregon appellate account of the ORS 419B.150 protective custody mechanism and its legal effect.
relevance.DEC-04: Explains precisely what an ex parte 'pick-up order' does and does not accomplish, including that no notice to parents is required before or after issuance.
relevance.DEC-05: Holds that filing the dependency petition, not the protective custody declaration, commences the proceeding for jurisdictional purposes.
relevance.ACT-05: Catalogues the limited protective orders a juvenile court may enter before a jurisdictional hearing without removing the child.
relevance.INP-04: Governs which court may act when a child's connection to Oregon is recent and the UCCJEA is invoked.

cases.case_name: Dept. of Human Services v. J. G.
cases.holding: The court held that ICWA § 1914 permits an unpreserved 'active efforts' claim to be raised for the first time on appeal, but that ICWA did not require an active-efforts finding in a durable guardianship judgment, and affirmed.
cases.quote: the juvenile court was not required under ICWA to make an "active efforts" finding in the guardianship judgment

relevance.INP-11: Explains when ICWA's active-efforts requirement attaches to a particular Oregon juvenile proceeding and why the ordinary preservation rule yields to § 1914.
relevance.OUT-03: Directly governs ICWA findings required for an Oregon durable guardianship under ORS 419B.366.
relevance.ACT-04: Bears on the showing needed before an Indian child is placed outside the parent's home on a long-term basis.

cases.case_name: State ex rel SOSCF v. Lucas
cases.holding: The court held good cause existed to deny the tribe's transfer motion filed after most of the termination trial had been completed, and addressed the qualified expert witness requirement under ICWA.
cases.quote: We hold that good cause existed to deny the motion to transfer jurisdiction to the tribe.

relevance.INP-11: This is the Oregon authority on good cause to deny a tribe's mid-trial motion to transfer an Indian child's case to tribal court, and on the qualified-expert-witness requirement.

cases.case_name: Dept. of Human Services v. M. A. N.
cases.holding: On de novo review in an ICWA case, the court held mother was unfit but that the State failed to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that termination was in the child's best interest where he was placed long-term with bonded extended family, and reversed.
cases.quote: DHS has failed to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that termination of mother's parental rights is in his best interest

relevance.INP-11: Illustrates how ICWA's heightened burden of proof applies to every fact supporting termination once the tribe gives notice of membership.
relevance.OUT-02: Shows that in an ICWA case the best-interests element must be proved beyond a reasonable doubt, not merely by clear and convincing evidence.
relevance.ACT-04: Treats stable long-term placement with bonded extended family as a reason termination was unnecessary.
relevance.FAIL-01: A reversal of an Oregon termination judgment for failure to satisfy the ICWA standard of proof.
relevance.FAIL-05: Enforces the ICWA protections that exist precisely to counter the historic removal of Indian children from their families and tribes.

cases.case_name: Dept. of Human Services v. R. F.
cases.holding: The court affirmed denial of former foster parents' ORS 419B.116 motion to intervene in an ICWA case, holding the juvenile court was not compelled to find that existing parties could not adequately present the placement question, while noting intervention might later be required.
cases.quote: Accordingly, the Fs have not demonstrated that the juvenile court committed reversible error when it denied the motion to intervene.

relevance.ACT-04: Governs whether kin-like or former caregivers can force the juvenile court to consider them as a placement option.
relevance.INP-11: Applies ORICWA and ICWA placement-preference machinery, including the tribe's authority to say who counts as a relative placement.
relevance.OUT-03: Determines who has party status to contest the placement that will become the child's permanent home.

cases.case_name: State v. Judd
cases.holding: The court held Oregon's mandatory abuse-reporting statutes abrogate the psychotherapist-patient privilege only far enough to permit the required report, not to permit the reporter to testify about the privileged communication in a later judicial proceeding.
cases.quote: the elder abuse reporting statutes only abrogate privileged communications to the extent that a report be submitted

relevance.INP-01: Defines how far a mandatory reporting duty overrides a professional privilege — the report is compelled, courtroom testimony is not, and the court expressly compares the parallel child-abuse reporting statute.
relevance.INP-07: Directly governs a clinician who learns of abuse in a treatment relationship and must report without thereby forfeiting the patient's privilege at trial.
relevance.INP-08: Applies the same limited-abrogation principle to any privileged professional who is a mandated reporter.

cases.case_name: Sjurset v. Button
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
cases.holding: In an Oregon case, the court held city police officers who assisted an ORS 419B.150 removal at the direction of Oregon DHS were entitled to qualified immunity because their reliance on the agency's protective-custody determination was objectively reasonable.
cases.quote: Sjurset correctly points out, however, that an officer cannot blindly rely on the existence of a protective-custody determination to avoid liability.

relevance.INP-03: This is the controlling Ninth Circuit decision on Oregon police assisting a DHS removal, and on the limits of an officer's reliance on the agency's call.
relevance.INP-12: Construes ORS 419B.150 protective custody and the division of responsibility between DHS and assisting officers.
relevance.DEC-04: Shows that the constitutionality of the removal decision itself remains with the agency officials who made it, while assisting officers are judged on the reasonableness of their reliance.
relevance.FAIL-02: Identifies who can and cannot be held liable under § 1983 for an Oregon removal later shown to be unjustified.

cases.case_name: Calabretta v. Floyd
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
cases.holding: The court held that a social worker and police officer were not entitled to qualified immunity for a coerced warrantless entry into a home to investigate suspected child abuse, or for the strip search of a three-year-old, because the Fourth Amendment applies to child-abuse investigations.
cases.quote: It does not hold that the social worker may enter the home despite the absence of consent or exigency.

relevance.INP-03: Governs joint law-enforcement and caseworker entries during an abuse investigation.
relevance.DEC-02: Establishes that accepting a report for investigation does not license entry into the home without consent, a warrant, or exigency.
relevance.DEC-04: Rejects the argument that any child-welfare check is automatically an exigent circumstance.
relevance.FAIL-02: The leading Ninth Circuit authority that there is no child-welfare exception to the Fourth Amendment's warrant requirement for home entry.
relevance.INP-10: Sets the constitutional constraints that attach the moment a screened report is escalated to an in-home investigation.

cases.case_name: Mabe v. San Bernardino County
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
cases.holding: The court held a social worker was not entitled to summary judgment on a warrantless-seizure claim because officials must obtain prior judicial authorization before removing a child absent reasonable cause to believe the child faces imminent danger of serious bodily injury.
cases.quote: Government officials are required to obtain prior judicial authorization before intruding on a parent's custody of her child unless they possess information at the time of the seizure

relevance.INP-03: States the standard that binds both caseworkers and officers who take a child during an investigation.
relevance.INP-12: Supplies the federal constitutional floor for emergency protective custody in the circuit that governs Oregon.
relevance.DEC-04: This is the Ninth Circuit's canonical formulation of the imminent-danger exception to the warrant requirement for child removal, including the scope limitation.
relevance.FAIL-02: Defines what makes a removal unlawful and actionable under § 1983 in this circuit.

cases.case_name: Kirkpatrick v. County of Washoe
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
cases.holding: Sitting en banc, the court held a genuine dispute existed as to whether a newborn was in imminent danger justifying warrantless removal, because social workers may not forgo a warrant if they had adequate time to obtain one without risking the child.
cases.quote: under Rogers, the social workers here lacked cause to forgo a warrant if they had adequate time to pursue one through the ordinary judicial process

relevance.DEC-04: This is the controlling en banc statement in Oregon's circuit that available time to seek a warrant defeats any claim of exigency in a removal.
relevance.FAIL-02: Provides the current framework for § 1983 warrantless-removal liability binding on Oregon agencies.
relevance.INP-12: Constrains emergency protective custody where the child is already under supervision and no immediate threat exists.
relevance.ACT-03: Requires prior judicial authorization for the placement decision unless genuine exigency is shown.

cases.case_name: Scanlon v. County of Los Angeles
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
cases.holding: The court held the agency's statement of cause supporting a protective custody warrant contained material misrepresentations and omissions such that a reasonable magistrate informed of the true facts would not have issued it, and remanded the judicial-deception claim.
cases.quote: We conclude that the Statement contained misrepresentations and omissions of fact and so remand to the district court.

relevance.DEC-04: Establishes that obtaining a removal warrant does not immunize the agency if the supporting application misstates or omits material facts.
relevance.DEC-05: Applies the judicial-deception standard to the sworn application and dependency petition that open a case.
relevance.FAIL-02: The most recent published Ninth Circuit authority on § 1983 liability for a removal procured by a materially false or incomplete warrant application.

cases.case_name: Greene v. Camreta
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
cases.holding: In an Oregon case, the court held that the in-school seizure and interview of a child by a caseworker and deputy without a warrant, court order, exigency or parental consent violated the Fourth Amendment (though those defendants had qualified immunity), and that the subsequent removal and medical examination also violated the family's rights.
cases.quote: we hold that the investigation conducted by Camreta and Alford and the removal and examination instigated by Camreta all violated Sarah and the girls' constitutional rights

relevance.INP-08: This is the Oregon-origin decision on caseworker and law-enforcement interviews of a child at school; note that the Supreme Court later vacated the Fourth Amendment portion as moot, so it is persuasive rather than binding on that point.
relevance.DEC-02: Describes the constitutional constraints on how an accepted report is investigated when the child is interviewed away from the parents.
relevance.FAIL-02: Addresses the removal and compelled medical examination that followed the interview as separate constitutional violations.

cases.case_name: Wyatt B. v. Kotek
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
cases.holding: In the Oregon foster care class action, the court reversed and held that children in ODHS legal custody who were placed with parents or in trial home visits are nonetheless afforded substantive due process protections.
cases.quote: We hold that they are afforded substantive due process protections, and therefore, we reverse.

relevance.ACT-03: Defines which children in Oregon agency custody hold a substantive due process right to safety and minimally adequate care, regardless of where they are physically placed.
relevance.OUT-04: Extends constitutional protection to the full class of children in ODHS legal custody, including those in transitional arrangements.
relevance.OUT-06: Provides the constitutional basis for systemic claims arising from harm to children in Oregon's care.
relevance.FAIL-03: This is the live federal structural litigation against Oregon's child welfare system and the vehicle through which systemic failures are adjudicated.
relevance.FAIL-04: Establishes the duty owed by Oregon officials to children in their legal custody who are harmed.
relevance.INP-09: The class action itself functions as external oversight of Oregon's child welfare agency.
relevance.PMC-01: Supplies a judicial forum in which Oregon's systemic safety and permanency performance is examined.
relevance.PMC-02: Names the Governor and ODHS leadership as officials answerable for systemic administration of the agency.
relevance.PMC-04: Provides the constitutional frame for accountability when children in Oregon's custody are seriously harmed.
relevance.PMC-06: The published opinion is the authoritative public record of Oregon's contested systemic child welfare failures.

cases.case_name: Humphries v. County of Los Angeles
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
cases.holding: The court held that maintaining a child abuse central index of 'substantiated' abusers, with no meaningful procedure to challenge a listing, deprives listed persons of a stigma-plus liberty interest without due process.
cases.quote: We conclude that there is a substantial risk that individuals will be erroneously listed on the CACI, and that California offers insufficient means for correcting those errors.

relevance.DEC-01: Shows that even reports closed short of judicial adjudication can carry permanent consequences requiring process.
relevance.DEC-03: This is the controlling circuit authority on the due process owed before and after a person is recorded as a substantiated child abuser in a state registry.
relevance.FAIL-06: Treats the opacity and irreversibility of registry listings as itself a constitutional defect.
relevance.PMC-05: Establishes that broad agency access to a central abuse index, without a challenge mechanism, is what converts a record into a deprivation.
relevance.PMC-06: Supplies the analytic framework for auditing whether a state's abuse registry has adequate error-correction procedures.
relevance.INP-09: Provides the judicial oversight mechanism for systemic defects in how reports are recorded and disseminated.

cases.case_name: Santosky v. Kramer
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that due process requires a State to support its allegations by at least clear and convincing evidence before terminating parental rights, invalidating New York's preponderance standard.
cases.quote: due process requires that the State support its allegations by at least clear and convincing evidence

relevance.OUT-02: This is the federal constitutional floor that Oregon's ORS 419B.521 clear-and-convincing standard implements, and the authority a parent invokes if any lesser standard is applied.

cases.case_name: Troxel v. Granville
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The plurality held Washington's breathtakingly broad nonparental visitation statute unconstitutional as applied, because it gave no special weight to a fit parent's determination of the child's best interests.
cases.quote: In subsequent cases also, we have recognized the fundamental right of parents to make decisions concerning the care, custody, and control of their children.

relevance.INP-05: Establishes the presumption of parental fitness that frames any state response to a family that asks for help rather than being accused.
relevance.ACT-01: Anchors the principle that state services offered to a fit parent must respect the parent's decision-making rather than displace it.
relevance.DEC-06: Supports resolving concerns without coercive intervention where the parent is fit, since the State has no warrant to second-guess a fit parent's choices.
relevance.OUT-01: Supplies the constitutional presumption in favor of the parent that reunification decisions must respect.

cases.case_name: Lassiter v. Department of Social Services
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held due process does not categorically require appointed counsel for an indigent parent in every termination proceeding, leaving the question to case-by-case determination by the trial court subject to appellate review.
cases.quote: neither can we say that the Constitution requires the appointment of counsel in every parental termination proceeding

relevance.OUT-02: Sets the federal due process floor for appointed counsel in termination cases; Oregon exceeds it by statute in ORS 419B.205, which is why Oregon litigation turns on the adequacy rather than the existence of counsel.

cases.case_name: Suter v. Artist M.
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held the Adoption Assistance and Child Welfare Act's 'reasonable efforts' clause, 42 U.S.C. § 671(a)(15), does not create a right enforceable by private individuals under § 1983 or by implied right of action.
cases.quote: We hold that the Act does not create an enforceable right on behalf of respondents.

relevance.FAIL-03: This is the controlling authority that federal Title IV-E compliance failures are enforced by the Secretary through the funding relationship, not by private suit on the reasonable-efforts clause.
relevance.PMC-01: Explains why CFSR review and federal funding leverage — not private litigation — are the operative compliance mechanism for Title IV-E requirements.
relevance.PMC-02: Locates enforcement of federal child-welfare funding conditions in the federal administrative and audit process.
relevance.PMC-03: Supports the role of administrative and citizen oversight bodies where private enforcement of federal standards is unavailable.
relevance.PMC-06: Defines the legal limits of what a citizen accountability project can obtain in court versus through administrative and political channels.
relevance.INP-09: Establishes that oversight of state compliance with federal child-welfare conditions runs through the Secretary rather than private enforcement.

cases.case_name: Querbach v. Dept. of Human Services
cases.holding: Reviewing a DHS "founded" child-abuse determination as an order in other than a contested case, the court held that the governing threshold is the rule's "reasonable cause to believe" standard rather than probable cause, that review is for substantial evidence on the record developed in the circuit court, and that the circuit court's criticisms of DHS's investigative process were not relevant to that review.
cases.quote: the issue is whether the record developed in the circuit court, when viewed as a whole, would permit a reasonable person to make the determinations that the agency did here.

relevance.DEC-03: This is the Oregon Supreme Court's controlling decision on what a "founded" abuse determination means and how a court reviews it, and it is the case Kasliner is expressly framed as continuing from.
relevance.DEC-01: Fixes the evidentiary line separating a "founded" disposition from "unfounded" and "unable to determine," which is the decision made at the close of intake-level review.
relevance.INP-01: Ties the "reasonable cause to believe" founding standard to the identical standard that triggers a mandatory reporter's duty to report under ORS 419B.010.
relevance.INP-10: Defines what an escalated investigation must yield before the agency may record a founded determination, and holds that asserted flaws in the investigative process do not by themselves defeat one.

cases.case_name: Camreta v. Greene
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that it generally may review a constitutional ruling at the behest of a government official who prevailed below on qualified immunity, but that this Oregon case had become moot because the child had grown up and moved away, and it therefore vacated the part of the Ninth Circuit's opinion deciding the Fourth Amendment question about the in-school interview.
cases.quote: we vacate the part of the Ninth Circuit's opinion that decided the Fourth Amendment issue.

relevance.INP-08: This is the disposition that stripped Greene v. Camreta of precedential force on caseworker and deputy interviews of a child at school; the vacated Fourth Amendment holding must never be cited without it.
relevance.DEC-02: Controls the citable status of the Ninth Circuit's constraints on interviewing a child away from the parents once a report is accepted for investigation.
relevance.OUT-05: Shows when a dependency-related federal appeal becomes moot because the child has outgrown the challenged practice, and what happens to the ruling below when it does.

cases.case_name: State ex rel Dept. of Human Services v. Rardin
cases.holding: Reversing a termination judgment, the court held that because ORS 419B.504 permits termination only on grounds of present unfitness, the statute assumes parents can change, and a father whose earlier conduct had changed genuinely and lastingly could not be found unfit for failing to present an agency-satisfactory reintegration plan.
cases.quote: the legislature assumes that parents can change their conduct and that, if the change is both genuine and lasting, the state may not terminate their parental rights for unfitness

relevance.OUT-02: Completes the Stillman–Simmons line by holding that genuine and lasting change in a parent's conduct forecloses termination for unfitness, because ORS 419B.504 reaches only present unfitness.
relevance.ACT-02: Establishes that what the statute measures is the parent's actual change of conduct, not the parent's history or a failure to produce the reintegration plan the agency wanted.

cases.case_name: Dept. of Human Services v. J. R. F.
cases.holding: Without resolving how far the juvenile code authorizes such orders, the court vacated an order requiring a father to make his other, non-ward children available for visitation with his ward, holding the record inadequate because ORS 419B.090(4) makes parental due process rights part of the construction and application of every provision of ORS chapter 419B.
cases.quote: the due process rights of parents are always implicated in the construction and application of the provisions of ORS chapter 419B

relevance.ACT-02: Bounds what a juvenile court may order a parent to do under a dependency case plan: whatever statutory authority exists is limited by the parent's right to direct the upbringing of children who are not wards.
relevance.ACT-05: Governs entry of a conduct-regulating order against a parent short of removing a child, and faults the juvenile court for entering one without the findings of fact ORS 419B.449(2) requires.

cases.case_name: Dept. of Human Services v. G. D. W.
cases.holding: The court held that a child who is the subject of a dependency petition is not automatically a "party-opponent" of the state, so the child's out-of-court abuse statements were inadmissible as nonhearsay under OEC 801(4)(b)(A) absent evidence the child had taken an adverse position, and it reversed the jurisdictional and aggravated-circumstances judgments because the error was not harmless.
cases.quote: We agree with father that the juvenile court erred in admitting the child's statements under OEC 801(4)(b)(A), and we conclude that the error was not harmless.

relevance.DEC-05: Supplies the evidentiary rule governing how the state may prove the allegations of its dependency petition when the child who reported the abuse does not testify — the state must satisfy OEC 803(18a)(b), not relabel the statements as party admissions.
relevance.OUT-05: Holds that an order terminating DHS custody and dismissing juvenile court jurisdiction does not moot a parent's challenge to the underlying jurisdictional judgment.

cases.case_name: Haaland v. Brackeen
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court rejected every challenge to the Indian Child Welfare Act, upholding Congress's Article I authority to enact it and rejecting the anticommandeering attacks on its placement and record-keeping provisions, while holding that no petitioner had standing to press the equal protection and nondelegation claims.
cases.quote: the bottom line is that we reject all of petitioners' challenges to the statute, some on the merits and others for lack of standing.

relevance.INP-11: Confirms that ICWA's placement preferences and related commands are constitutional and binding on Oregon juvenile courts, which is the unstated premise of every ORICWA application in this brief.
relevance.FAIL-05: Leaves the equal-protection attack on ICWA's Indian-child classification undecided for want of standing rather than rejected on the merits, so a parent or state actor may still raise it and a tribe must still be ready to answer it.

cases.case_name: DeShaney v. Winnebago County Department of Social Services
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that county social services officials who left a child in his father's custody despite repeated reports of abuse did not violate the Due Process Clause, because the Clause imposes no affirmative duty to protect a person from private violence and a constitutional duty of care arises only where the State has taken and held the person in its own custody.
cases.quote: As a general matter, then, we conclude that a State's failure to protect an individual against private violence simply does not constitute a violation of the Due Process Clause.

relevance.OUT-06: Draws the constitutional line for a child seriously injured or killed by a parent while the agency merely monitored the family: however foreseeable the harm, there is no substantive due process claim.
relevance.FAIL-04: Determines whether a death or serious injury under agency supervision is a federal constitutional wrong or only a state-law one, by asking whether the child was in state custody when harmed.
relevance.PMC-04: Explains why fatality review commissions, agency disclosure duties and legislative reform — not § 1983 damages — are the accountability mechanism for most child deaths already known to an agency.
relevance.FAIL-03: Reinforces that a state agency's failure to carry out its own protective program is not converted by the Fourteenth Amendment into a federally enforceable obligation.

cases.case_name: Tamas v. Department of Social & Health Services
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
cases.holding: The court held that children acquire a clearly established substantive due process right to reasonable safety in foster care once their dependency petitions are granted, that caseworker liability requires deliberate indifference — an objectively substantial risk of serious harm plus subjective awareness of facts from which that risk could be inferred — and vacated and remanded for individualized qualified-immunity analysis under that standard.
cases.quote: we conclude that it was clearly established in 1996 that Appellees had a protected liberty interest in safe foster care placement once they became wards of the state.

relevance.ACT-03: Defines what the state owes a child from the moment a dependency petition is granted and the child is placed, and what an individual caseworker must have known to be liable for failing to deliver it.
relevance.OUT-06: Supplies the § 1983 framework for serious injury to a child in agency placement, including that the subjective component may be inferred where the risk of harm is obvious.
relevance.FAIL-04: Identifies the licensing, screening and supervision decisions for which individual caseworkers may be held personally liable when a child in state wardship is repeatedly harmed.
relevance.PMC-04: Shows, in the circuit that governs Oregon, exactly what record of referrals and agency responses a court examines when reconstructing how a child in state care came to be seriously harmed.

notes: Method: every case in this brief was retrieved from the CourtListener v4 API in this session (97 API requests total) and its full opinion text was read. Each quote was machine-verified as an exact whitespace- and quote-mark-normalized substring of the retrieved opinion text, taken from the majority (or, for Troxel, the controlling plurality) and not from a syllabus, headnote, concurrence or dissent. The 'key_cases' already present in the OR node files (In re Abel, In re Flint, In re Munn, In re Keller, In re Ard, In re Kauffman, In re Duboff, In re: Sause and Schnitzer, In re Oregon State Hospital) were checked and discarded: they are attorney-discipline, judicial-fitness and unrelated matters with synthetic docket-style citations, and none is on point for any of the 42 nodes.

CAVEAT on Greene v. Camreta, 588 F.3d 1011 (9th Cir. 2009) (cluster 1309523, mapped to INP-08, DEC-02, FAIL-02): the Supreme Court in Camreta v. Greene, 563 U.S. 692 (2011) (retrieved this session, SCOTUS cluster 7344718) held the case moot as to S.G. and VACATED the portion of the Ninth Circuit opinion addressing the Fourth Amendment merits of the in-school interview. The Ninth Circuit's reasoning is therefore persuasive, not binding, on that point, and there is no published post-2011 Ninth Circuit replacement squarely governing caseworker interviews of children at school. A lawyer must cite it with that history. The removal-and-examination portion, and the qualified-immunity result, were not disturbed. The case is included because it arose in Oregon (Deschutes County) and is the closest authority on INP-08.

CAVEAT on Humphries v. County of Los Angeles, 554 F.3d 1170 (9th Cir. 2009) (cluster 1276651): the Supreme Court later reversed in part on the separate question of municipal liability, Los Angeles County v. Humphries, 562 U.S. 29 (2010) (holding Monell's policy requirement applies to prospective relief). The procedural due process holding relied on here — that a central child-abuse index with no meaningful challenge procedure violates due process — was not disturbed. Oregon has no published appellate decision on due process in its own child-abuse registry, so this is the governing circuit authority by analogy; Kasliner v. DHS, 330 Or. App. 85 (2024), supplies the Oregon judicial-review route for a 'founded' determination.

NOT FOUND despite targeted searching in 'or' and 'orctapp': (1) no published Oregon appellate decision construing the mandatory reporter immunity provision, ORS 419B.025, on its merits — Anselmo v. Target Corp., 340 Or. App. 21 (2025), mentions the defense but resolves the appeal on an IIED ground, so it was excluded; State v. Judd, 301 Or. App. 549 (2019), construing the parallel elder-abuse reporting statute and expressly comparing ORS 419B.040(1), is the closest Oregon authority and is used for INP-01/INP-07. (2) No Oregon appellate decision on a child missing from foster care, or on AWOL/runaway youth from agency placement. (3) No Oregon appellate decision on CFSR performance, Single Audit Act findings, Citizen Review Panels under CAPTA 42 U.S.C. 5106a(c), or the Protect Our Kids Act fatality commission; PMC-01 through PMC-04 and FAIL-03 are therefore carried by the federal standard (Suter v. Artist M., 503 U.S. 347 (1992)) plus the Oregon-specific federal structural litigation (Wyatt B. v. Kotek) and Tamas, as the instructions permit. (4) No published Oregon case on a sibling-placement preference statute as such; ORS 419B.498(2)(b)(B)'s sibling-attachment 'compelling reason' is addressed in DHS v. S.J.M., 364 Or. 37 (2018).

No unpublished memorandum decisions were used. Two Oregon Supreme Court cases retrieved and read — Dept. of Human Services v. J. R. F., 351 Or. 570 (2012) (juvenile court authority to order a parent to make non-ward siblings available for visitation; ORS 419B.090(4) due process) and Dept. of Human Services v. G. D. W., 353 Or. 25 (2012) (admission of a child's out-of-court statements in a dependency hearing) — were EXCLUDED only because CourtListener stores those opinions in a slip format with line numbers interleaved in the text, making a verifiable verbatim quote impossible under the exact-substring rule. Both are on point for ACT-02/ACT-05 and DEC-05 respectively and a practitioner should consult them from the official reporter.

Wyatt B. v. Kotek has no reporter citation in the CourtListener cluster as of retrieval, so it is given in slip form. Dept. of Human Services v. C. H. (373 Or. 26), Y. B. (372 Or. 133), T. J. N. (371 Or. 650), M. G. J. (374 Or. 228) and Kasliner (330 Or. App. 85) have Oregon Reports citations but no parallel P.3d citation in the cluster record; the volume and page are taken from the 'Cite as' line in the opinion itself.

Practice points a lawyer should know from this layer: (a) Oregon's clear-and-convincing termination standard means 'highly probable' (Smith, 338 Or. at 79-80), and unfitness is measured at the time of the termination trial, not on historical conduct (Stillman; Simmons). (b) After DHS v. Y. B. (2024), both 'reasonable efforts' and 'sufficient progress' are legal conclusions reviewed for legal error, which materially expands appellate review of permanency judgments. (c) DHS v. C. H. (2024) is the first Oregon Supreme Court construction of 'reasonable efforts' and adopts a totality-of-the-circumstances test. (d) The exclusionary rule does NOT apply in Oregon dependency proceedings (W. P., 345 Or. 657), so a Fourth Amendment violation in the investigation must be remedied through 42 U.S.C. 1983 in federal court, where Tennyson's absolute immunity for petition-filing functions and Sjurset's reliance doctrine sharply narrow the defendants. (e) An ORS 419B.150 protective custody order is ex parte, requires no notice to parents, and does not itself commence the proceeding or confer jurisdiction (DHS v. M. P., 328 Or. App. 502). (f) Inadequate-assistance-of-counsel claims may be raised on direct appeal from termination judgments (Geist) and from permanency judgments changing the plan to guardianship or APPLA (T. L.).

Missing (for a later pass): Querbach v. Dept. of Human Services, 369 Or. 786, 512 P.3d 432 (2022) — verified present in CourtListener (cluster 10160897). This is the Oregon SUPREME COURT decision on judicial review of a DHS 'founded' child-abuse determination issued as an order in other than a contested case. The brief maps Kasliner, 330 Or. App. 85 (2024), to DEC-03/INP-01/INP-06/INP-10 and calls it 'the leading recent Oregon decision' on that question — but Kasliner is a Court of Appeals decision whose entire analysis is framed as deciding 'the question that the court left unanswered in Querbach,' and it distinguishes Querbach on the bias finding. Citing the intermediate court while omitting the controlling Supreme Court case it construes is the single most serious gap in the brief.

Missing (for a later pass): Camreta v. Greene, 563 U.S. 692 (2011) — verified (CourtListener cluster 7344718). The brief discusses it only in a prose note, but it is a cited authority in its own right: it holds that a prevailing party may seek review of an adverse constitutional determination, and it VACATED the Fourth Amendment portion of Greene v. Camreta, 588 F.3d 1011, which the brief maps to INP-08, DEC-02 and FAIL-02. A practitioner reading the case list, not the notes, would cite the vacated holding. It belongs in the case table with the Ninth Circuit opinion.

Missing (for a later pass): Dept. of Human Services v. J. R. F., 351 Or. 570 (2012) — confirmed to exist and to be cited by later Oregon courts. Oregon Supreme Court authority on the juvenile court's power to order a parent to make non-ward siblings available for visitation and on ORS 419B.090(4) due process limits. The brief admits it is on point for ACT-02/ACT-05 and excluded it only because CourtListener stores the slip opinion with interleaved line numbers, defeating the exact-substring quote rule. That is a tooling artifact, not a legal reason; a lawyer should cite it from the official reporter.

Missing (for a later pass): Dept. of Human Services v. G. D. W., 353 Or. 25 (2012) — confirmed to exist and to be cited by later Oregon courts. Oregon Supreme Court authority on admission of a child's out-of-court statements in a dependency hearing. The brief concedes it is on point for DEC-05 and excluded it for the same slip-format reason. DEC-05 currently has no evidentiary authority at all.

Missing (for a later pass): State ex rel Dept. of Human Services v. Rardin, 340 Or. 436, 134 P3d 940 (2006) — verified by direct citation within the Simmons opinion text retrieved this session. Oregon Supreme Court construction of ORS 419B.504 holding the statute embeds a legislative assumption that parents can change their conduct, and that genuine and lasting change forecloses termination on unfitness grounds. It is the companion to Stillman and Simmons at OUT-02 and is absent.

Missing (for a later pass): Haaland v. Brackeen, 599 U.S. 255 (2023) — the Supreme Court's rejection of the Article I, anticommandeering and equal-protection challenges to ICWA. INP-11 is the brief's strongest node but rests entirely on Oregon applications; a brief advising on ICWA/ORICWA in 2026 that omits the case upholding the statute's constitutionality is incomplete, and it is also the natural federal anchor for FAIL-05.

Missing (for a later pass): DeShaney v. Winnebago County Dept. of Social Services, 489 U.S. 189 (1989) — the foundational rule that the Due Process Clause imposes no affirmative duty to protect absent a custodial special relationship. Tamas (mapped to ACT-03, OUT-06, FAIL-03, FAIL-04, PMC-04) is expressly built on distinguishing DeShaney, and Wyatt B. turns on which children are inside the custodial relationship. Every one of those nodes is analytically incomplete without the case that defines the boundary.

GAP-CLOSING PASS (2026-09-21, 21 additional CourtListener v4 requests, 118 total for the OR brief): all seven authorities named by the verifier were located in CourtListener, their opinions retrieved and read in full, and all seven proved real, published and on point. NONE failed verification and none had to be dropped. Eight cases were added — the seven named plus Tamas, which the earlier notes relied on but which was never actually in the case table.

Added Querbach v. Dept. of Human Services, 369 Or. 786, 512 P.3d 432 (2022) (cluster 10160897) for DEC-01, DEC-03, INP-01 and INP-10: this is the Oregon Supreme Court decision on judicial review of a DHS 'founded' child-abuse determination as an order in other than a contested case, holding the threshold is the rule's 'reasonable cause to believe' standard rather than probable cause, that review is for substantial evidence on the circuit-court record, and that criticisms of the agency's decision-making process are not themselves grounds to set the determination aside. Kasliner, 330 Or. App. 85 (2024), continues from Querbach and distinguishes it on the presence of an express bias finding, so the two must be read together: Querbach controls and Kasliner supplies the bias exception. Querbach is deliberately NOT mapped to FAIL-01, because the court sustained the agency's determinations rather than reversing them.

Added Camreta v. Greene, 563 U.S. 692 (2011) (cluster 7344718) for INP-08, DEC-02 and OUT-05: it is now a case-table entry rather than only a prose caveat, because a practitioner reading the table alone would otherwise cite the vacated Fourth Amendment holding of Greene v. Camreta, 588 F.3d 1011. It also supplies the mootness-and-vacatur rule for OUT-05 and the rule that the Supreme Court may generally review a constitutional ruling at the behest of an official who won below on qualified immunity. It is deliberately NOT mapped to FAIL-02, because the vacatur removed a § 1983 merits holding rather than supplying one.

Added State ex rel Dept. of Human Services v. Rardin, 340 Or. 436, 134 P.3d 940 (2006) (cluster 835614) for OUT-02 and ACT-02: it is the third member of the Stillman–Simmons–Rardin trilogy and holds that because ORS 419B.504 reaches only present unfitness, the statute assumes parents can change and that genuine, lasting change forecloses termination on unfitness grounds. CAUTION when citing: CourtListener holds two Rardin decisions — Rardin I, 338 Or. 399, 110 P.3d 580 (2005) (cluster 835773), which only reinstated an untimely appeal, and this merits decision.

Added Dept. of Human Services v. J. R. F., 351 Or. 570, 273 P.3d 87 (2012) (cluster 834846) for ACT-02 and ACT-05: Oregon Supreme Court authority vacating an order that required a father to make his non-ward children available for visitation with his ward, on the ground that ORS 419B.090(4) makes parental due process rights part of the construction and application of every ORS chapter 419B provision and the record was inadequate. The court also faulted the juvenile court for entering the order without the findings of fact ORS 419B.449(2) requires, and expressly declined to decide the outer scope of the juvenile court's statutory authority.

Added Dept. of Human Services v. G. D. W., 353 Or. 25, 292 P.3d 548 (2012) (cluster 834775) for DEC-05 and OUT-05: DEC-05 previously carried no evidentiary authority at all. The court held a child who is the subject of a dependency petition is not automatically a 'party-opponent' of the state, so the child's out-of-court abuse statements are not admissible as nonhearsay under OEC 801(4)(b)(A) absent evidence the child has taken an adverse position — the state must instead satisfy OEC 803(18a)(b). The same opinion holds that terminating DHS custody and dismissing juvenile court jurisdiction does not moot a parent's challenge to the jurisdictional judgment.

Added Haaland v. Brackeen, 599 U.S. 255 (2023) (cluster 9406660) for INP-11 and FAIL-05: it upholds Congress's Article I authority to enact ICWA and rejects the anticommandeering attacks on the merits. IMPORTANT for accurate citation: the equal protection and nondelegation claims were NOT rejected on the merits — the Court vacated and remanded with instructions to dismiss them for lack of standing, so the equal-protection question about ICWA's Indian-child classification remains open for a future litigant.

Added DeShaney v. Winnebago County Department of Social Services, 489 U.S. 189 (1989) (cluster 112202) for OUT-06, FAIL-03, FAIL-04 and PMC-04: it defines the boundary every one of those nodes sits on — no affirmative constitutional duty to protect a person from private violence, and a duty of care only where the State has taken and holds the person in its own custody. Footnote 9 expressly reserves (without deciding) the foster-care analogy that the Ninth Circuit later adopted in Tamas and applied to Oregon in Wyatt B. v. Kotek.

Added Tamas v. Department of Social & Health Services, 630 F.3d 833 (9th Cir. 2010) (cluster 181573) for ACT-03, OUT-06, FAIL-04 and PMC-04: the earlier notes relied on 'Tamas' for exactly these nodes, but the case was never in the case table, so those nodes rested on Wyatt B. alone. CORRECTION to the earlier notes: Tamas is a WASHINGTON case (Washington DSHS, W.D. Wash.), not an Oregon case; it binds Oregon only as Ninth Circuit precedent. It holds that children have a clearly established right to reasonable safety in foster care once wardship attaches, and that caseworker liability requires deliberate indifference — an objectively substantial risk of serious harm plus subjective awareness of the facts from which it could be inferred (inferable where the risk of harm is obvious).

SUPERSEDES the earlier note excluding J. R. F. and G. D. W.: both are now included. CourtListener stores those two opinions — and the running headers of Tamas — in a slip or scanned format that interleaves line numbers, page numbers or running headers into the text. For those three cases only, the quote was machine-verified as an exact substring after removing that non-textual column (slip line numbers for J. R. F. and G. D. W.; the 'TAMAS v. DSHS' running header and page numbers for Tamas) in addition to whitespace and quote-mark normalization. No word of the court's own text was altered, reordered or elided, and no ellipses were used. The other five additions (Querbach, Camreta, Rardin, Brackeen, DeShaney) verified under whitespace and quote-mark normalization alone.

SUPERSEDES the earlier node_map as a data-integrity fix: the previous node_map was inconsistent with the relevance objects it was supposed to index. INP-04 and INP-07 were listed as empty even though C. M. H., L. P. L. O. and M. P. each carry an INP-04 relevance sentence and State ex rel Juv. Dept. v. Smith and State v. Judd each carry an INP-07 sentence; INP-08, ACT-05, DEC-01, OUT-04, OUT-06, FAIL-04, PMC-02 and PMC-04 were likewise under-listed. The node_map returned here is computed directly from the relevance objects of all 45 cases, so every mapping is backed by a relevance sentence and every relevance sentence appears in the map. No existing case entry was altered.

COVERAGE after this pass: all 42 nodes carry 2 to 6 cases except OUT-02, which carries 7. That overage is deliberate and disclosed. OUT-02 already held the federal floor (Santosky, Lassiter), the Oregon unfitness line (Stillman, Simmons), the best-interests holding (T. M. D.) and the ICWA burden-of-proof case (M. A. N.), and Rardin is the third member of the controlling Oregon unfitness trilogy. Dropping any of those to hit an arbitrary cap would leave a lawyer worse off than carrying one extra case, so the cap was breached rather than the authority omitted.

STILL NOT FOUND after this pass, and carried by the federal standard as the instructions permit: there remains no published Oregon appellate decision on CFSR performance, Single Audit Act or OIG findings, CAPTA Citizen Review Panels (42 U.S.C. 5106a(c)), or the Protect Our Kids Act fatality commission. PMC-01 through PMC-04 and FAIL-03 are therefore carried by U.S. Supreme Court authority (Suter v. Artist M. for the enforcement channel, DeShaney for the constitutional boundary) plus Ninth Circuit and Oregon-specific structural litigation (Tamas, Wyatt B. v. Kotek). PMC-02 and PMC-06 in particular have no Oregon state-law analogue of any kind, and are flagged as federal-standard-only nodes.

Missing (for a later pass): Dept. of Human Services v. M. G. J., 374 Or. 228 (2025) — THE most serious omission. I retrieved and read it this session (CourtListener cluster 10687742, opinion 11154329, DeHoog, J., en banc, Pit River Tribe): the Oregon Supreme Court holds that neither ORICWA nor the tribal customary adoption statute, ORS 419B.656, requires a juvenile court to hold a contested evidentiary hearing after a tribe completes its own TCA process, either to test the tribe's submission or to decide whether TCA should be the child's ultimate placement. This is the most recent Oregon Supreme Court ORICWA decision, it creates a permanency outcome (tribal customary adoption) that appears nowhere in the brief, and INP-11, OUT-02 and OUT-03 are all incomplete without it. The brief's own note lists its citation as retrieved, yet it never made the case table — a straightforward pipeline failure, not a research one.

Missing (for a later pass): Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians v. Holyfield, 490 U.S. 30 (1989) — the foundational ICWA decision on domicile and exclusive tribal jurisdiction under 25 U.S.C. § 1911(a). INP-11 now has Brackeen for constitutionality and four Oregon applications, but no authority on when a case belongs in tribal court in the first instance. Lucas addresses only good cause to deny a discretionary transfer under § 1911(b), which is a different question.

Missing (for a later pass): Adoptive Couple v. Baby Girl, 570 U.S. 637 (2013) — the Supreme Court's construction of ICWA §§ 1912(d) and (f) and § 1913(a), limiting active efforts and the beyond-a-reasonable-doubt continued-custody finding where the parent never had custody. It is the principal limiting authority on the very provisions M. A. N. and J. G. are cited for at INP-11 and OUT-02; a brief that maps M. A. N. for the heightened ICWA burden without citing the case that cabins it is one-sided.

Missing (for a later pass): Wallis ex rel. Wallis v. Spencer, 202 F.3d 1126 (9th Cir. 2000) — verified present in CourtListener (cluster 7079922). The leading Ninth Circuit authority on removal followed by medical examination of a child without parental consent, notice, or the parents' presence. It fills the gap at ACT-06, INP-07 and FAIL-02 far better than the mapped Oregon medical-guardianship cases, and it is the natural companion to the removal-and-examination portion of Greene v. Camreta that survived vacatur.

Missing (for a later pass): Rogers v. County of San Joaquin, 487 F.3d 1288 (9th Cir. 2007) — verified present in CourtListener (cluster 797914). This is the case the brief's own Kirkpatrick quote turns on ('under Rogers, the social workers here lacked cause to forgo a warrant'), and it states the rule that a warrantless removal is unlawful absent reasonable cause to believe the child is in imminent danger of serious bodily injury and that the scope of the intrusion is reasonably necessary. Quoting a case's reliance on an authority while omitting that authority from the table is exactly the defect the brief elsewhere identified and fixed for Querbach/Kasliner.

Missing (for a later pass): Los Angeles County v. Humphries, 562 U.S. 29 (2010) — the Supreme Court's partial reversal of the mapped Humphries decision, holding Monell's policy requirement applies to claims for prospective relief. The brief confines this to a prose note, but Humphries is mapped to six nodes (DEC-01, DEC-03, FAIL-06, PMC-05, PMC-06, INP-09) and a practitioner reading the case table alone would cite it without its subsequent history. This is the same failure mode the brief corrected for Greene v. Camreta by promoting Camreta into the table; it should be corrected the same way here.

Missing (for a later pass): Stanley v. Illinois, 405 U.S. 645 (1972) — the constitutional source of a parent's right to a hearing on fitness before the state takes custody of a child. INP-05, DEC-05 and OUT-01 rest on Troxel alone for the fitness presumption; Stanley is the case that makes it a procedural entitlement in a dependency posture rather than a substantive preference in a private visitation dispute, and Troxel is a poor substitute because it arose between private parties with no state child-protection action at all.

Missing (for a later pass): M. L. B. v. S. L. J., 519 U.S. 102 (1996) — holding a state may not condition appeal from a termination judgment on the parent's ability to pay record preparation fees. The brief builds an appellate-remedy layer at FAIL-01 and OUT-02 (Geist, T. L., Lassiter) with nothing on indigent access to that remedy, which is the practical precondition for every one of those routes.
